title: Plus or Minus to Hit a Target
statement:
You get a list nums of non-negative integers and an integer target. Put a + or a − in front of every number, keep their order, and add them all up.

Return how many of the 2ⁿ sign choices give exactly target. Sign choices are counted separately even when they give the same sum, so +0 and −0 are two different choices.

examples.why: +2 + 1 − 1 and +2 − 1 + 1. The two 1s sit at different positions, so these are two choices.
+0 + 3 and −0 + 3. A zero doubles the count instead of being ignored.
Every signed sum of 4 and 2 is even, so 1 is out of reach.

hints: Decide the signs one number at a time. After the first i numbers, what is the only thing about your choices that still matters for the future?
Only the running sum matters. Let dp[i][s] be the number of ways the first i numbers reach sum s. Sums range from −total to total, so shift the index by total.

dp[i][s] = dp[i−1][s − x] + dp[i−1][s + x] for x = nums[i−1]. Shorter: if P is the sum of the plus group, P − (total − P) = target, so count subsets with sum (total + target) / 2, a 0/1 knapsack in one array.

explain.intuition:
Trying all 2ⁿ sign choices works for 20 numbers, but many choices pass through the same running sum, and from there the rest of the problem is identical. So group them. Let dp[i][s] be the number of sign choices for the first i numbers whose sum is s. The last decision is the sign of x = nums[i−1]: with +, the earlier numbers had to reach s − x; with −, they had to reach s + x. So dp[i][s] = dp[i−1][s − x] + dp[i−1][s + x], starting from dp[0][0] = 1. Sums can be negative, so store s at index s + total. The table is (n + 1) × (2·total + 1).

A bit of algebra makes it smaller. Split the numbers into a plus group with sum P and a minus group with sum total − P. Then P − (total − P) = target, so P = (total + target) / 2. The question becomes: how many subsets have sum P? If total + target is odd or negative there are none. Otherwise it is a 0/1 knapsack count: one array ways, and for each number sweep x downward so that each number is used at most once. A zero makes ways[x] += ways[x], which doubles every count, matching +0 and −0.
steps: Let total = sum(nums). If |target| > total or total + target is odd, return 0.
For each number v: for x from P down to v, ways[x] += ways[x − v].
pitfalls: Skipping zeros or treating +0 and −0 as one choice. The second example then gives 1 instead of 2.
Forgetting the parity and range checks. (total + target) / 2 for [4, 2], target = 1 is 3.5, and for a target beyond ±total it is an index outside the array.
Sweeping upward in the one-array version. That lets a number join the plus group twice.

solutions.title: Try both signs for every number
solutions.idea: Recurse on the index and the running sum, adding and subtracting each number. Visits all 2ⁿ choices.

solutions.title: Table of prefixes × running sums
solutions.idea: dp[i][s] = ways for the first i numbers to reach s, with s shifted by total so negative sums fit. Each cell adds the + and − cases.

solutions.title: Count subsets that form the plus group
solutions.idea: The plus group must sum to (total + target) / 2. Count those subsets with a 0/1 knapsack in one array, sweeping downward.

followups: Return one valid sign assignment, or report that none exists.
Numbers may now also be multiplied by 0 (left out). How does the recurrence change?
nums has 40 numbers with values up to 10⁹. The sum table is too wide. What would you do instead? (Hint: split the list in half.)
